title: Process Crash Detection (Linux)
exclusions: Detects Linux kernel syslog records containing the documented `process[PID]: segfault at ...` signature. It does not detect clean exits, application exceptions, systemd unit failures without a kernel segfault record, OOM kills, container-only logs, or crashes reported solely by `systemd-coredump`. It does not prove that a core file was written, because core creation depends on signal disposition, resource limits, and core-handler configuration.
evidence: Saved search `linux_process_segfault_5m`, its versioned SPL and schedule, alert history, the matching raw kernel event with extracted process and PID, and a snapshot of the Universal Forwarder file-input configuration. A linked incident or approved test record supplies operational disposition; these artefacts demonstrate monitoring activity, not regulatory compliance.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Index one synthetic `linux_messages_syslog` event on host `crash-test`: `Jul 28 09:00:00 crash-test kernel: crashprobe[4242]: segfault at 0 ip 0000000000401136 sp 00007ffd00000000 error 4 in crashprobe[400000+1000]`. The completed five-minute bucket must return one row with `process_name=crashprobe`, `process_ids=4242`, and `crash_count=1`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Index `Jul 28 09:02:00 crash-test systemd[1]: crashprobe.service: Deactivated successfully.` with the same sourcetype, plus `Jul 28 09:03:00 crash-test kernel: crashprobe[4243]: exited normally`. Neither event contains the kernel segfault signature, so the saved search must return zero rows for `crash-test` in that bucket.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog` events from the active Linux system log, commonly `/var/log/messages`; the file path must be confirmed per distribution. Collect with a Universal Forwarder file monitor deployed alongside the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (Splunkbase 833). Required indexed fields are `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`; the SPL extracts `process_name`, `process_id`, `fault_address`, `instruction_pointer`, `stack_pointer`, `error_code`, and optional `fault_object`. The `os` index name is a local convention.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) for managed Linux collection, plus the Splunk platform's built-in `linux_messages_syslog` sourcetype. The detection does not depend on undocumented add-on field extractions.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog "kernel:" "segfault at"
| rex field=_raw "(?i)kernel:\s+(?<process_name>[^\[\r\n]+)\[(?<process_id>\d+)\]:\s+segfault at\s+(?<fault_address>\S+)\s+(?:ip|rip)\s+(?<instruction_pointer>\S+)\s+(?:sp|rsp)\s+(?<stack_pointer>\S+)\s+error\s+(?<error_code>\d+)(?:\s+in\s+(?<fault_object>[^\[]+)\[[^\]]+\])?"
| where isnotnull(process_name) AND isnotnull(process_id)
| eval process_name=trim(process_name), fault_object=if(isnull(fault_object),"unknown",trim(fault_object))
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count as crash_count values(process_id) as process_ids values(fault_address) as fault_addresses values(error_code) as error_codes values(fault_object) as fault_objects values(source) as sources by _time host process_name
| where crash_count>=1
| sort 0 -_time host process_name
description: Detects kernel-reported Linux process segmentation faults whose raw syslog text matches `process[PID]: segfault at ...`. Each result represents one host, extracted process name, and five-minute bucket, and appears when that bucket contains at least one qualifying event; the row retains crash count, PIDs, fault addresses, error codes, implicated objects, and log sources.
value: Rapid notification of a native-process memory fault can shorten service-restoration and defect-triage time by directing responders to the affected host, executable label, and PID before log rotation removes the first failure record. Grouped recurrence also helps teams distinguish an isolated bad invocation from a crash loop that warrants rollback or vendor escalation.
implementation: Monitor the distribution's active kernel/system log with a Universal Forwarder, assign the built-in `linux_messages_syslog` sourcetype, and route it to the locally selected operating-system index. Verify the Red Hat-style kernel signature and every extracted field before saving `linux_process_segfault_5m`; run every five minutes over the preceding completed five-minute bucket and trigger on any result.
visualization: Show a timechart of `crash_count` by `process_name`, a table with `_time`, `host`, `process_name`, `process_ids`, `error_codes`, and `fault_objects`, and a host/process recurrence panel over 24 hours. Link each row to the raw event, service status, deployment history, and available `coredumpctl` metadata; label all counts as kernel-reported segfault events rather than distinct outages.

knownFalsePositives:
The signature is strong evidence of a real kernel-reported segfault; the scenarios below are false-positive operational pages, not fabricated crashes.

1. **Approved crashprobe fault-injection test** — A release qualification or resilience exercise may deliberately run `crashprobe`. Match the exact host, process name, test window, and change record before suppressing it.

2. **GDB or ABRT reproduction session** — An engineer may intentionally reproduce a vendor defect while collecting a core. Confirm the active incident, operator, and test host; route the result to the existing case instead of opening a duplicate outage.

3. **systemd restart policy containing impact** — A worker can segfault and be immediately replaced by `Restart=on-failure`. Check `systemctl show <unit> -p NRestarts,ActiveState,SubState` and service health; downgrade notification priority only when the replacement is healthy, because the crash remains genuine.

4. **Duplicate syslog paths** — Monitoring both `/var/log/messages` and a relayed copy can index the same kernel line twice. Compare `_raw`, `host`, source paths, and `_indextime`, then fix the overlapping Universal Forwarder inputs rather than hiding the process.

5. **Truncated Linux task name** — The kernel task label can be shorter or less specific than the executable path, causing unrelated workers to share `process_name`. Distinguish them with `process_ids`, the service inventory, and `COREDUMP_EXE` from `coredumpctl` when available.

**Suppression mechanism:** if approved tests require suppression, add a locally governed `linux_process_crash_exceptions.csv` lookup keyed by exact `host` and `process_name`, with ISO-8601 `start_time`, `end_time`, owner, reason, and ticket. Filter only events inside that time-bound exception; reject wildcards and expired entries.
reviewer: documentation review against Splunk, Linux, systemd, and Red Hat primary sources
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and scope

Deploy a supported release of the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) with the Universal Forwarder, and confirm compatibility with the deployed Splunk platform before rollout. The Splunkbase listing warns that upgrades across add-on version 6.0 changed defaults and configuration files, so test upgrades outside production. Grant the infrastructure-monitoring role read access to the selected operating-system index and permission to create the saved search; no administrative role is required to run this SPL.

Identify the log that actually receives kernel messages on each supported distribution. Red Hat commonly writes them to `/var/log/messages`; another distribution may use `/var/log/syslog`, `/var/log/kern.log`, or only the systemd journal. Do not monitor all candidate paths blindly. This implementation covers a text file whose events preserve the `kernel: process[PID]: segfault at ...` record. A journal-only design needs a separately documented journal collection path and field validation.

## 1. Collect and verify the kernel record

Create a local file-monitor override under the deployment app's `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf`; never edit `default/inputs.conf`. Point the monitor stanza at the verified active file, set `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`, and route it to the approved event index. The catalogue uses `index=os`, but that name is a deployment convention. Restart the Universal Forwarder as required by Splunk's configuration-file workflow, then inspect the effective stanza with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`.

Search `index=os sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog source="/verified/path" earliest=-15m` on a representative host. Confirm `_time`, `_raw`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`, and compare a test record with the host's source log. Splunk documents `linux_messages_syslog` as its pretrained source type for standard Linux `/var/log/messages` records. Do not claim add-on-normalized crash fields: this SPL deliberately extracts the Red Hat-documented process, PID, addresses, error code, and optional object from `_raw`.

Check ingestion latency by comparing the event timestamp with `_indextime`. A five-minute schedule is unsafe when routine latency exceeds the search delay; correct forwarding or widen the delayed completed-bucket window without overlapping dispatches.

## 2. Understand and save the detection

The base search first requires both `kernel:` and `segfault at`, then `rex` accepts the documented `ip`/`sp` or `rip`/`rsp` forms. Events that fail to produce both `process_name` and `process_id` are removed rather than grouped under null. `bin` creates five-minute buckets, and `stats` produces one row per `_time`, `host`, and `process_name`; `crash_count` is the number of matching kernel records, not the number of affected users or outages.

Save the search as `linux_process_segfault_5m`. Schedule it every five minutes over the preceding completed five-minute bucket, for example `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, after confirming that this delay covers normal ingestion. Trigger when the result count is greater than zero. The threshold is therefore at least one matching event per host/process/five-minute bucket. A single segfault is retained because a critical daemon can fail once and stay down; tune routing and urgency by service ownership and restart outcome instead of discarding first occurrences. Throttle duplicate notifications by `host` and `process_name` for 30 minutes while retaining every dispatch result for recurrence analysis.

There is no CIM search for this implementation. The source is raw Linux syslog, and neither Splunkbase 833 nor the built-in sourcetype establishes a documented CIM mapping for this kernel fault record. Do not label the extracted fields as Endpoint data-model fields without a separately tested normalization design.

## 3. Validate the search logic

Use a nonproduction index or controlled test input; do not crash a production process merely to test an alert. Index the exact positive event from `controlTest` with `sourcetype=linux_messages_syslog`. Confirm one row in the correct five-minute bucket, `process_name=crashprobe`, `process_ids=4242`, `error_codes=4`, and `crash_count=1`. Verify that the optional `fault_object` becomes `crashprobe` and that the source file is retained in `sources`.

Index both negative records and confirm zero rows. Also test a valid segfault record without an `in object[...]` suffix: it must still return with `fault_objects=unknown`. Test malformed text lacking a numeric PID and confirm it is rejected. These are documentation-level synthetic controls, not evidence that the search has executed against a customer workload.

If an approved end-to-end host test is necessary, use an organization-approved crash fixture on an isolated test host, record the change ticket, and compare the Splunk event with `journalctl -k` or the active system log. Where `systemd-coredump` is enabled, `coredumpctl info 4242` can corroborate signal and executable metadata, but absence of a retained core does not invalidate the kernel record.

## 4. Alert, visualize, and respond

Send the alert to the owning Linux or application queue with `_time`, `host`, `process_name`, `process_ids`, `error_codes`, `fault_objects`, and a link to the raw event. Page immediately only when the service inventory marks the process as critical or health checks show impact. Build a 24-hour recurrence chart and a table that exposes raw-event drilldown; never title the chart "all process crashes" because this search covers segmentation faults only.

The runbook should identify the service and owner, check `systemctl status` and `systemctl show <unit> -p NRestarts,ActiveState,SubState`, inspect deployment and package changes, and determine whether restart restored service. Preserve the original log and available core metadata before restarting repeatedly. Escalate recurring faults with executable/package version, exact timestamp, PID, error code, implicated object, and core/backtrace location. Do not automate process killing, rollback, or core-file deletion from this alert.

## 5. Suppress and troubleshoot safely

Treat a matching kernel line as a real segfault even when operational impact is expected. For an approved test, use the local `linux_process_crash_exceptions.csv` convention with exact `host` and `process_name`, bounded `start_time` and `end_time`, owner, reason, and ticket. Apply the lookup before alerting, retain suppressed rows for review, and reject wildcard or permanent exceptions.

No events usually means the wrong file is monitored, kernel messages remain only in journald, routing uses another `index=`, or the search role lacks access. Null extractions indicate a message format outside the documented Red Hat form; inspect `_raw` and add a source-specific parser only after collecting representative examples. Inflated counts usually indicate overlapping file and relay inputs. Missing core files can result from signal handling, `RLIMIT_CORE`, `kernel.core_pattern`, storage policy, or `systemd-coredump` retention and must not be diagnosed as a Splunk extraction failure.
grandmaExplanation: Linux can leave a precise log note when a program crashes because it touched memory incorrectly. We collect that note so the team knows which machine and program failed and can check whether the service recovered.
